thread:
Olivia: Quick follow-up from the afternoon sync — thinking about simplifying the operator surface for Dedicated GPU pool autoscaling. Sketching a concrete split and wanted reactions.

Mike: +1 to simplification. The current admit/lease surface has too many cross-calls with control-plane logic. What are you proposing?

Olivia: Make the operator minimal: node lifecycle, warmup orchestration, and resource-level traces. Move admission, headroom math, burst accounting, and fallback policy into a centralized controller that emits an opaque "intent" bundle. Operator only consumes intent and returns a tiny execution handle.

Tara: So we replace admit tokens with an intent object. How is that better?

Olivia: Two wins: 1) intent bundles are declarative and enumerate fallback paths (lower-quantized SKU, region, model-variant), so operator doesn't need model-awareness. 2) the execution handle is light: handle_id, expiry_ts, progress_hint. Operator maps handle -> nodes and reports warmup/eviction, no policy decisions.

Mike: Decoupling sounds good. Concern: debugging. If operator doesn't pick the fallback, ops needs to know why a fallback was chosen. Where's that decision recorded?

Devon: We should emit structured audit events from the controller: intent.submitted, intent.decision (chosen_fallback), intent.applied. Operator emits resource events: handle.allocated, warmup.done, handle.released. infra-bot can stitch them in the console.

Olivia: Exactly. Keep policy in controller timeline; operator emits node-level traces only.

Tara: Tradeoff: controller becomes thicker and holds more trust. For Private deployments (customer-managed control plane) we need to keep portability. How do we handle that?

Mike: We can ship a compatibility shim that runs next to the operator in Private. The public controller remains the source of truth in Hosted. For Private, the shim validates/augments intents locally and exposes the same operator gRPC. That keeps operator surface unchanged.

Olivia: Edge-case: burst-lane admission. Today operator takes and tracks burst credits. Under thin-operator, controller computes burst eligibility and attaches a burst_hint to the intent. Operator enforces eviction/grace windows and reports credit_burn metrics.

Devon: Centralizing credits makes accounting easier, but billing still needs per-tenant burn metrics. Add metric hooks on handle lifecycle: credit_burned, credit_source, and ledger_id. Operator should emit these when handle completes.

Mike: For quality rollback and model safety, intent should include a safety_testset_id and a quality_gate threshold. Controller can mark intent.failed and apply fallback if live telemetry crosses the threshold; operator just reports token counts and quality telemetry hooks.

Tara: API shapes proposal: POST /intents -> {intent_id, submitted_at}. GET /intents/{id} -> {status, applied_fallbacks, handle}. Operator gRPC: AcceptIntent(intent_proto) -> ExecutionHandle(handle_id, expiry, progress_hint). ReleaseHandle(handle_id).

Olivia: Yes — keep the operator gRPC tiny for performance. Richer controller REST API for troubleshooting/UX.

Devon: Also handle graceful reclaim: if operator needs to evict nodes, it should send an eviction_notice with grace_window and optionally a prewarm_ticket for controller to attempt reschedule. That keeps tail-latency bounded.

Mike: Sounds practical. Next steps: I'll draft an RFC with lifecycle diagrams, API sketches, and a migration plan for existing admit/lease users. Aim for review next week?

Olivia: Please include a Private deployment compatibility section. Tagging infra-bot to capture the event list for observability. :eyes: 

infra-bot: captured events stub: intent.submitted, intent.decision, intent.fallback_applied, handle.allocated, handle.warmup_done, handle.released, handle.eviction_notice. See /observability/events for schema.

Tara: I'll add SLO implications and a migration checklist (admit token deprecation, metrics mapping).

Olivia: Great. If anyone has objections to the thin-operator model, post them on the RFC PR.

Mike: Will do.
